question: Why is the box topology on an infinite product not compact?

turns.response:
{"topic": "Non-compactness of the box topology on infinite products",
 "summary": "On an infinite product $\\prod_i X_i$, the box topology takes arbitrary products of open sets as basic opens, which is far finer than the product topology. Even a product of compact spaces like $\\{0,1\\}^{\\mathbb{N}}$ fails to be compact: because each coordinate can be controlled independently and simultaneously, one can build an open cover whose sets each pin down infinitely many coordinates, so no finite subcollection can reach every point. The essence is that box-open sets are too small — you can isolate points enough that finiteness never suffices.",
 "visualize": true,

 "beats": [
   {"title":"Stack the coordinates forever","claim":"Introduce the infinite product space, e.g. sequences of 0s and 1s, drawn as an infinite row of coordinate slots."},
   {"title":"Open boxes down every slot","claim":"A box-open set restricts EVERY coordinate at once — show a basic open as a choice in each of infinitely many slots, contrasting with product topology which restricts only finitely many."},
   {"title":"Boxes can be tiny everywhere","claim":"Because all coordinates are constrained, a box can be as small as a single point's neighborhood — the topology is very fine, points get nearly isolated."},
   {"title":"Cover with point-pinning boxes","claim":"Construct an open cover where each box pins down infinitely many coordinates, so each box captures only a thin slice of the product."},
   {"title":"Finitely many can't fill it","claim":"Any finite subfamily still leaves coordinates free to disagree — exhibit a point escaping every chosen box, so no finite subcover exists."},
   {"title":"Compactness fails by fineness","claim":"Conclude: even a product of compact factors is non-compact in the box topology precisely because the opens are too small to be covered finitely."}
